summary: During two successive Hajj seasons, delegations from the tribes of Aws and Khazraj in Yathrib (Madinah) met secretly with the Prophet ﷺ at a valley called al-Aqabah in Mina, pledging their belief in Islam, their allegiance, and ultimately their military protection — paving the way for the Hijrah.
narrative:
The First Pledge of Aqaba took place in approximately 621 CE, during the Hajj season. The Prophet ﷺ had for several years been presenting Islam to tribal delegations that came to Makkah for pilgrimage, but met with repeated rejection. The Aws and Khazraj tribes of Yathrib, however, were in a state of exhaustion from their prolonged inter-tribal warfare — culminating in the devastating Battle of Bu'ath — and were receptive to a message of unity and divine authority.

Ibn Hisham records that twelve men from the Khazraj and one or two from the Aws came to the Prophet ﷺ at al-Aqabah and took a pledge known as the 'Pledge of Women' (bay'at al-nisa') because it was similar in content to the pledge that would later be taken from women — no shirk, no theft, no fornication, no killing of children, no slander, and no disobedience to the Prophet ﷺ in good matters. The Prophet ﷺ sent Musab ibn Umayr (RA) back with them to Yathrib as the first Muslim teacher and ambassador — a role in which he proved extraordinarily effective. Within a year, Islam had spread widely through the tribes of Yathrib, with entire households accepting the faith.

The Second Pledge of Aqaba, in 622 CE (the year of the Hijrah), was a far larger and more consequential gathering. Ibn Hisham preserves a detailed account: seventy-three men and two women from the Aws and Khazraj assembled secretly at al-Aqabah in the dead of night. The Prophet ﷺ came with his uncle al-Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib, who had not yet embraced Islam but came as a protective witness for his nephew. Al-Abbas spoke first, telling the delegation: 'If you believe you can truly fulfill what you are inviting him to and protect him against all who oppose him, then take him. But if you intend to abandon him after taking him out, then leave him now, for he has honor and protection here.'

The leaders of the delegation — including Asad ibn Zurara and Abd Allah ibn Rawaha — affirmed their commitment. They asked: 'What is for us if we fulfill this pledge?' The Prophet ﷺ replied: 'Paradise.' They pledged to protect him as they would their own women and children. This pledge contained a military commitment — defense against all enemies — which distinguished it sharply from the First Pledge. Ibn Hisham records that al-Abbas ibn Ubadah (not al-Abbas the uncle) offered to attack the Quraysh with swords the very next morning, but the Prophet ﷺ declined, saying: 'We have not been commanded to do that yet.'

The Prophet ﷺ then asked the delegation to name twelve leaders (nuqaba') — nine from the Khazraj and three from the Aws — who would be responsible for their people. He said to them: 'You are the guarantors of your people, just as the disciples of Isa ibn Maryam were guarantors for him, and I am the guarantor for my people.' This organisational structure was the foundation of the governance model that would emerge in Madinah.

The Quraysh learned of the meeting shortly after and were furious. But the delegation had already departed for Yathrib, and the Hijrah was now set in motion. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir both describe the Second Aqaba Pledge as the pivotal moment that made the Hijrah possible — the formal contractual basis for the establishment of the first Muslim polity.
